source_text: Deos non esse quos colit vulgus hinc notum est. Reges olim fuerunt, qui ob regalem memoriam coli apud suos postmodum etiam in morte coeperunt. Inde illis instituta templa, inde, ad defunctorum vultus per imaginem detinendos, expressa simulacra; et immolabant hostias, et dies festos dando honore celebrabant. Inde posteris facta sunt sacra, quae primis fuerant assumpta solatia. Et videamus an stet haec apud singulos veritas. Melicertes et Leucothea praecipitantur in maria, et fiunt postmodum maris numina. Castores alternis moriuntur ut vivant. Aesculapius ut in Deum surgat fulminatur. Hercules ut hominem exuat Oeteis ignibus concrematur. Apollo Admeti pecus pavit. Laomedonti muros Neptunus instituit, nec mercedem operis infelix structor accepit. Antrum Jovis in Creta visitur, et sepulchrum ejus ostenditur, et ab eo Saturnum fugatum esse manifestum est. Inde Latium de latebra ejus nomen accepit. Hic litteras imprimere, hic signare nummos in Italia primus instituit: inde aerarium Saturni vocatur. Et rusticitatis hic cultor fuit: inde falcem ferens senex pingitur. Hunc fugatum hospitio Janus exceperat; de cujus nomine Janiculum dictum est, et mensis Januarius institutus est. Ipse bifrons exprimitur, quod, in medio constitutus, annum incipientem pariter et recedentem spectare videatur. Mauri vero manifeste reges colunt, nec ullo velamento hoc nomen obtexunt. Inde per gentes et provincias singulas varia deorum religio mutatur, dum non unus ab omnibus deus colitur, sed propria cuique majorum suorum cultura servatur. Hoc ita Alexander Magnus insigni volumine ad matrem suam scribit metu suae potestatis proditum sibi de diis hominibus a sacerdote secretum, quod majorum et regum memoria servata sit, inde colendi et sacrificandi ritus inoleverit. Si autem aliquando dii nati sunt, cur non hodieque nascuntur? nisi si forte Jupiter senuit, aut partus in Junone defecit. Cur vero deos putas pro Romanis posse, quos videas nihil pro suis adversus eorum arma valuisse? Romanorum enim vernaculos deos novimus. Est Romulus pejerante Proculo deus factus, et Picus, et Tiberinus, et Pilumnus, et Consus, quem Deum fraudis vel ut consiliorum deum, coli Romulus voluit postquam in raptum Sabinarum perfidia provenit. Deam quoque Cloacinam Tatius et invenit et coluit, Pavorem Hostilius atque Pallorem. Mox a nescio quo Febris dedicata, et Acca et Flora meretrices. [Interdum vero deorum vocabula apud Romanos finguntur, ut sit apud illos et Viduus deus, qui anima corpus viduet, qui quasi feralis et funebris intra muros non habetur; et nihilominus, quia extorris factus, damnatur potius Romana religione, quam colitur. Est et Scansus ab ascensibus dictus, et Forculus a foribus, et a liminaribus Limentinus, et Cardea a cardinibus et ab orbitatibus Orbona]. Hi dii Romani. Caeterum Mars Thracius, et Jupiter Creticus, et Juno vel Argiva vel Samia vel Poena, et Diana Taurica, et deorum mater Idaea, et Aegyptia portenta, non numina: quae utique si quid potestatis habuissent, sua ac suorum regna servassent. Plane sunt apud Romanos et victi penates, quos Aeneas profugus advexit. Est et Venus calva, multo hic turpius calva quam apud Homerum vulnerata.
pass_a_gloss: It is known from this that the gods, which the crowd worships, do not exist. Kings were once, who, on account of the royal memory, began to be worshiped by their own people even after death. From this, temples were established for them, and from this, images were made to retain the faces of the dead; and they were offering sacrifices, and they were celebrating festival days by giving honor. From this, sacred rites were made for posterity, which were first taken up as consolations. And let us see whether this truth stands among individuals. Melicertes and Leucothea were thrown into the sea, and they became later sea gods. The Castors die alternately so that they may live. Aesculapius was struck by lightning so that he might rise to God. Hercules was cremated in the Oeteian fires so that he might shed his human form. Apollo herded Admetus' cattle. Neptune built walls for Laomedon, and the unhappy builder did not receive the reward for his work. The cave of Jupiter in Crete is visited, and his tomb is shown, and it is clear that Saturn was fugitive from him. From this, Latium received its name from his hiding place. He first established the practice of minting coins and stamping letters in Italy: from this, the treasury is called Saturn's. And he was a cultivator of rusticity: from this, he is painted as an old man carrying a sickle. This fugitive was received in hospitality by Janus; from whose name the Janiculum is said, and the month of January is established. He himself is depicted as two-faced, because, having been established in the middle, he seems to look equally at the beginning and the ending of the year. The Moors, indeed, clearly worship kings, and they do not cover this name with any veil. From this, the religion of the gods changes through the individual nations and provinces, while not one god is worshiped by all, but each one's own culture of their ancestors is preserved. Alexander the Great writes to his mother in a remarkable volume, revealing a secret about the gods, which was betrayed to him by a priest, out of fear of his power, that the memory of ancestors and kings has been preserved, and from this, the rites of worship and sacrifice have grown. But if the gods were ever born, why are they not born today? Unless perhaps Jupiter has grown old, or childbirth has failed in Juno. Why, indeed, do you think that the gods can do anything for the Romans, whom you see have not been able to do anything for their own against the arms of their enemies? For we know the Roman gods are home-born. Romulus was made a god by the perjury of Proculus, and Picus, and Tiberinus, and Pilumnus, and Consus, whom Romulus wanted to be worshiped as the god of fraud or as the god of counsel, after his perfidy was proven in the abduction of the Sabines. Tatius also found and worshiped the goddess Cloacina, and Hostilius worshiped Fear and Pallor. Soon, Fever was dedicated by someone, and Acca and Flora, prostitutes. Sometimes, indeed, the names of the gods are invented among the Romans, so that there is a god Viduus among them, who widows the soul from the body, who, as if funereal and mournful, is not held within the walls; and nevertheless, because he was made an outcast, he is condemned rather than worshiped by Roman religion. There is also Scansus, named from the ascents, and Forculus from the doors, and Limentinus from the thresholds, and Cardea from the hinges, and Orbona from the orbits. These are the Roman gods. Moreover, Mars is Thracian, and Jupiter is Cretan, and Juno is either Argive or Samian or Carthaginian, and Diana is Taurian, and the mother of the gods is Idaean, and the Egyptian portents are not divine powers: which, indeed, if they had any power, would have preserved their own and their people's kingdoms. Clearly, there are among the Romans also conquered household gods, which the fugitive Aeneas brought. And there is Venus, bald, much more shamefully bald here than wounded in Homer.

pass_b_english: We can see from this that the gods the common people worship do not exist. There were once kings who, because their subjects wanted to preserve the royal memory, began to be worshiped even after death. That is how temples were founded for them, and how images were carved to keep the faces of the dead before the living. People offered sacrifices and celebrated festival days to honor them. In time, these practices became sacred rites for later generations, though they began as consolations for the first mourners. Let us test whether this same pattern holds true in individual cases.

Melicertes and Leucothea were thrown into the sea and afterward became sea deities. The Castors die on alternate days so that they may live. Aesculapius was struck by lightning so that he might rise to the rank of a god. Hercules was burned on the fires of Mount Oeta so that he might shed his mortal nature. Apollo herded cattle for Admetus. Neptune built walls for Laomedon, yet the unhappy builder never received his wages. People still visit the cave of Jupiter in Crete, and his tomb is shown there; it is also clear that Saturn fled from him. Latium took its name from that hiding place. Saturn was the first to introduce the practice of minting coins and stamping letters in Italy; that is why the treasury bears his name. He also cultivated the rustic life, which is why he is depicted as an old man carrying a sickle. Janus welcomed this fugitive with hospitality; the Janiculum hill is named after him, and the month of January was instituted in his honor. Janus is portrayed with two faces because, standing at the midpoint of the year, he appears to look at both the year beginning and the year ending.

The Moors openly worship kings, making no attempt to disguise the fact. Consequently, the religion of the gods varies from nation to nation and province to province, since no single god is worshiped by all; instead, each people preserves the ancestral cult of its own forebears. Alexander the Great attests to this in a remarkable letter to his mother. He writes that a priest, terrified of Alexander's power, betrayed a secret about the gods: the memory of ancestors and kings was preserved, and from that preservation the rites of worship and sacrifice arose.

But if the gods were ever born, why are they not still being born today? Unless, perhaps, Jupiter has grown old, or childbirth has failed in Juno. Why do you suppose the gods can help the Romans when you see they could do nothing to save their own people against enemy arms? We know the Roman gods are homegrown. Romulus became a god through the perjury of Proculus. So did Picus, Tiberinus, Pilumnus, and Consus — whom Romulus wanted worshiped as the god of fraud, or else as the god of counsel, after his treachery in the abduction of the Sabine women was exposed. Tatius discovered and worshiped the goddess Cloacina. Hostilius worshiped Fear and Pallor. Later, Fever was dedicated by someone unknown, along with Acca and Flora, who were prostitutes. Sometimes the Romans even invent divine names: there is a god Viduus, who severs the soul from the body; considered funereal and mournful, he is not admitted within the walls. Yet because he is an outcast, Roman religion condemns him rather than worships him. There is also Scansus, named from ascents; Forculus, from doors; Limentinus, from thresholds; Cardea, from hinges; and Orbona, from childlessness. These are the Roman gods.

Beyond them, Mars is Thracian, Jupiter is Cretan, Juno is either Argive, Samian, or Carthaginian, Diana is Taurian, the Mother of the Gods is Idaean, and the Egyptian portents are not divine powers at all — if they had any power, they would have preserved their own kingdoms and those of their people. Clearly, the Romans also possess conquered household gods, which the fugitive Aeneas brought with him. And there is Venus, depicted as bald — far more shamefully bald here than when Homer merely shows her wounded.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the Latin text. Pass A and Pass B both correctly handle the complex list of Roman deities and their etymologies. Pass B provides a more fluent rendering of the historical and mythological nuances (e.g., 'Oeteis ignibus' as 'fires of Mount Oeta' and 'Orbona' as 'childlessness' which is a valid interpretation of the root/context). All clauses, including the specific etymological claims for Scansus, Forculus, Limentinus, Cardea, and Orbona, are preserved.
